reviews.notes: Arjuna opening query: contrast between renunciation of actions (sannyāsa) and practice of selfless action (yoga).
Krishna reply: both paths lead to liberation, but karma-yoga is superior to mere renunciation of work.
Definition of true sannyāsin: one who neither hates nor desires, untouched by dualities; note [FN#8].
Reconciliation of Sankhya and Yoga: the immature regard them as separate, but mastering one yields the fruit of both.
Identity of ultimate goal: the realm attained by Sankhyans is reached by Yogins; who sees them as one sees truly.
Difficulty of renunciation without karma-yoga; seamlessly combined with 5.7 in shared source span.
Attributes of the pure-hearted yogayukta whose self is one with all life; shared source span with 5.6.
Consciousness of the seer of truth: "I do nothing at all" while seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, breathing, sleeping.
Speaking, releasing, grasping, opening and shutting eyes, knowing senses operate among sense-objects.
Offering deeds to Brahman without attachment: sin taints him no more than water adheres to an enamelled lotus-leaf.
Yogins perform action solely with body, mind, intellect, and senses, shedding egoism for inner purification.
The disciplined seeker renouncing fruits gains steadfast peace; the selfish worker driven by desire is fettered.
The embodied soul mentally renouncing works rests serenely in the "city of nine gates" [FN#9], neither acting nor causing action.
The Sovereign of the world creates neither agency, nor action, nor karmic reward; Nature alone operates.
The Lord takes neither the good nor evil deeds of humans; spiritual darkness clouds knowledge, breeding delusion.
When ignorance is dispelled by Self-knowledge, that supreme wisdom shines like the rising sun.
Souls centered on That, merged in That, going to the state of no-return; includes bracketed poetic gloss.
Universal vision of the wise (samadarśinaḥ): seeing Brahman equally in scholar, cow, elephant, dog, and outcast.
Mortal world is conquered here on earth by minds established in equal vision, resting in sinless Brahman.
Neither overjoyed by pleasant fortune nor shaken by sorrow, steady of intellect, abiding untroubled in Brahman.
Detached from outward sensory impressions, one discovers bliss within; united with Brahman, he tastes eternal peace.
Sensual pleasures are but fertile wombs of grief with beginnings and endings; the wise mind finds no delight in them.
Blessed and happy is the person who masters the violent surge of lust and wrath here on earth before shedding the body.
The yogin who possesses inner joy, inner peace, and inner light becomes Brahman and enters Brahma-nirvana.
Liberation attained by seers whose sins are cleansed, doubts ended, minds governed, rejoicing in welfare of all.
Brahma-nirvana is ever present for ascetics freed from passion and anger, self-subdued, and knowing the Soul.
Meditation technique: excluding external contacts, focusing gaze between brows, equalizing inward and outward breath.
With senses, heart, and mind disciplined, intent on liberation, casting off desire, fear, and wrath, one is ever free.
Knowing Krishna as enjoyer of sacrifice, supreme Lord of all worlds, and lover of all living beings brings final peace.

chapterFindings: Arnold tightly intertwines the difficulty of renunciation (5.6) and the qualities of the yogayukta (5.7) into a single period ("Yet such abstraction, Chief! Is hard to win without much holiness... A Yogayukt--he is a Saint who wends Straightway to Brahm. Such an one is not touched By taint of deeds"), accurately mapped as a shared source span.
Verses 5.8 and 5.9 divide the sensory activities catalogue cleanly between 5.8 ("seeing, hearing... slumbers") and 5.9 ("or talks, Holds fast...") across line 999.
Verse 5.17 preserves Arnold bracketed poetic gloss "[Who will may have this Light; Who hath it sees.]" alongside the translation.
All 29 canonical references are fully accounted for with complete source span coverage.
